s: Where the Civil War's first shots were fired
w: Still unfinished when Confederate guns opened fire on April 12, 1861, this sea fort at the harbor mouth became the place the Civil War started. Built on an artificial island after the War of 1812 exposed America's coastal defenses as inadequate, it never did get finished - the damage from that first battle saw to that.
_facts: incomplete sea fort at the mouth of Charleston Harbor
site of the battle that started the Civil War, April 12, 1861
built on an artificial island from 1829 in response to the War of 1812
never completed to its original plan, now run by the National Park Service

w: Nicknamed 'The Ship That Would Not Die,' this WWII destroyer survived D-Day, then off Okinawa took on wave after wave of kamikaze pilots in the most sustained kamikaze attack of the war - and kept firing. She is a National Historic Landmark now, moored at Patriots Point.
_facts: Allen M. Sumner-class destroyer, commissioned February 1944
earned the nickname 'The Ship That Would Not Die' during D-Day and the Battle of Okinawa
withstood the most unrelenting kamikaze air attack in history
now a National Historic Landmark museum ship at Patriots Point

s: The Cooper River's third-longest cable-stayed span
w: Its 1,546-foot main span makes this the third-longest cable-stayed bridge in the Western Hemisphere, strung across the Cooper River since 2005. Locals still call it the Cooper River Bridge out of habit, but two decades on its white cables have become the skyline shot every Charleston postcard needs.
_facts: cable-stayed bridge over the Cooper River connecting Charleston to Mount Pleasant
main span of 1,546 feet, third longest among cable-stayed bridges in the Western Hemisphere
opened in 2005, designed by Parsons Brinckerhoff
considered an icon of Charleston, colloquially the Cooper River Bridge

s: A Founding Father's quieter Lowcountry retreat
w: Charles Pinckney helped draft the US Constitution, then came home to this Lowcountry farm he called Snee Farm - part plantation, part retreat. He had already survived the Revolutionary War and a stint as a prisoner up north before he signed his name to the founding document.
_facts: preserves a portion of Charles Pinckney's Snee Farm plantation and country retreat
Pinckney fought in the Revolutionary War, was held prisoner, and was a delegate to the constitutional convention
designated a National Historic Landmark in 1973, National Historic Site in 1988

s: A fort with double billing: military and political
w: Tucked onto the northeastern tip of James Island, this state-owned site carries a rare double designation - military and political significance both - for a stretch of Charleston Harbor most visitors never think to look for.
_facts: state-owned historic site of military and political significance
located on the northeast point of James Island, Charleston County

s: A cotton merchant's mansion turned Masonic hall
w: A cotton merchant built this Second Empire mansion in 1886, only for Charleston's Scottish Rite Masons to buy it in 1920 and bolt on an auditorium for 600 members. That wing is long gone, torn down once its connecting corridor outlived its use - but the mansion survived, into Historic Hotels of America.
_facts: built 1886 for cotton merchant Francis Silas Rodgers
Second Empire style
purchased 1920 by the Scottish Rite Cathedral Association, which added a 600-seat auditorium later removed
listed in Historic Hotels of America since 2003

n: Greek Orthodox Church of the Holy Trinity
s: A Byzantine dome from the Grand Central tile firm
w: A Presbyterian architect designed this Byzantine-style sanctuary for Charleston's Greek Orthodox community in the early 1950s, its central dome built by the Guastavino tile firm of Massachusetts. The icons came all the way from Athens; one priest, Nicholas Trivelas, held the pulpit for nearly fifty years straight.
_facts: present church built 1950-1953, designed by architect Harold Tatum in Byzantine style
central dome built by the Guastavino Tile Company of Woburn, Massachusetts
icons by Photios Kontoglou of Athens
Rev. Nicholas Trivelas served as pastor for nearly five decades from 1947

s: The fort that gave South Carolina its palmetto flag
w: Built from palmetto logs, the first fort on this spot bounced cannonballs so well it gave South Carolina both its nickname and the palm tree on its flag. The British held it under a different name during their occupation, but it came back as Fort Moultrie, honoring the commander who beat them here in the first place.
_facts: fortifications on Sullivan's Island built to protect Charleston
first fort, Fort Sullivan, built of palmetto logs, inspired the Palmetto State nickname and flag
renamed for General William Moultrie
known as Fort Arbuthnot during British occupation 1780-1782

n: Cathedral of Saint John the Baptist
s: Rebuilt after fire, finished a century later
w: Replacing a cathedral the Civil War burned to the ground in 1861, this one broke ground in 1890 and did not get its steeple bells - cast in France, like the stained glass - until it was finally completed in 2010. The mother church of Charleston's Catholic diocese seats 720 and keeps a crypt beneath the nave.
_facts: mother church of the Roman Catholic Diocese of Charleston, designed by Patrick Keely
construction began 1890 to replace a cathedral burned down in 1861, dedicated 1907
stained glass made in France, steeple bells cast in France, completed 2010
upper church seats 720 worshippers and includes a crypt

w: The only independent Huguenot church left in America, this Gothic Revival sanctuary traces its congregation back to the 1680s, when French Protestants fled persecution after the Edict of Nantes was revoked. The 1844 building still runs its liturgy in the 18th-century French rite - just translated into English now.
_facts: only independent Huguenot church in the United States
congregation traces origins to the 1680s, when Huguenots fled persecution in France
built 1844, oldest Gothic Revival church in South Carolina, National Historic Landmark
services still follow an 18th-century French liturgy, conducted in English

s: A tiny fort, six weeks of Civil War combat
w: A tiny masonry fort built in the middle of Charleston Harbor in 1810, its entire Civil War combat career lasted six weeks as a makeshift prisoner-of-war camp before it faded into disuse. It has sat quietly in the harbor ever since, part of the National Register since 1970.
_facts: small masonry fortification built by the US government in Charleston Harbor in 1810
used briefly, about six weeks, as a POW camp and artillery position during the Civil War
listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1970

s: An art museum, delayed a decade by its own family
w: James Gibbes left Charleston $100,000 in his will for 'the erection of a suitable building' - and his own relatives fought it in court for years. New York's Supreme Court upheld the gift in 1901; the Beaux-Arts gallery rose soon after with a Tiffany-style dome, and now holds over 10,000 works, mostly American.
_facts: established as the Carolina Art Association in 1858
James Shoolbred Gibbes donated $100,000 for the building, contested in court by his nieces and nephews
New York Supreme Court upheld the gift in 1901, Beaux Arts building designed by Frank Pierce Milburn with a Tiffany-style dome
collection of over 10,000 works, principally American

s: Home to a railroad baron, then his governor son
w: Built in 1820 as a Charleston double house, this became home to two men named William Aiken - a railroad baron father, then his governor son - and stands today as the city's best-preserved complex of antebellum domestic buildings. Donated to the Charleston Museum in 1975, it has been a house museum since 1995.
_facts: built 1820 in the Wraggborough neighborhood, a Charleston double house
home of William Aiken, owner of the South Carolina Canal and Railroad Company, then his son Gov. William Aiken Jr.
considered the best-preserved complex of antebellum domestic structures in Charleston
donated to the Charleston Museum in 1975, operated as a house museum by Historic Charleston Foundation since 1995
